name: Bruce Castle
text: Your train passes near Bruce Castle, on the train's {side}, a 16th-century manor house and one of the oldest surviving English brick houses. The postal reformer Sir Rowland Hill lived there; it is now a museum, and its grounds, a park since 1892, are Tottenham's oldest.

name: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
text: Your train passes near Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened on April 3rd 2019 on the site of the club's old ground, White Hart Lane, and land beside it. With 62,850 seats it is the largest club ground in London, and its pitch slides away to reveal an artificial one for American football.

name: Pymmes Park
text: Your train passes near Pymmes Park, on the train's {side}, named after Pymmes House, built there by William Pymme in 1327. William Cecil, Lord Burghley, bought the estate in 1582; the council bought it for a public park, which opened in 1906.

name: All Saints' Church, Edmonton
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, Edmonton, on the train's {side}, first recorded in the 12th century and rebuilt in the 15th; its west tower still has its medieval outside. The essayist Charles Lamb and his sister Mary, a writer, are buried there.

name: Barclays Bank, Enfield
text: Your train passes near Barclays Bank in Enfield, on the train's {side}, where the world's first cash machine was put in, in 1967. A gold-coloured cash machine and a plaque have marked the spot since 2017; the building itself was finished in 1897.

name: Ripaults Factory
text: Your train passes near the Ripaults Factory, on the train's {side}, a listed art deco building designed by A. H. Durnford for a firm that made electrical cables and parts for motor vehicles. Built in the 1930s, it has since been used by the lorry maker MAN and then a builders' merchant.

name: St James' Church, Enfield Highway
text: Your train passes near St James' Church, Enfield Highway, on the train's {side}, consecrated on October 15th 1831. Built by subscription as a chapel of ease, it was the first Anglican church in the parish of Enfield besides the parish church itself.

name: Clapton Cinematograph Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Clapton Cinematograph Theatre, on the train's {side}, opened on December 16th 1910 and one of the earliest purpose-built cinemas in London. It was built after new safety rules of 1909, as film then was highly flammable, and seated 750.

name: Walthamstow Marshes
text: Your train passes Walthamstow Marshes, on the train's {side}, one of the last pieces of near-natural wetland in Greater London. In 1909 Alliott Verdon Roe made the first all-British powered flight across them, in his Roe I Triplane; he went on to found Avro.

name: Markfield Beam Engine
text: Your train passes near the Markfield Beam Engine, on the train's {side}, built in 1886 to pump Tottenham's sewage towards Beckton. Its flywheel is 27 feet across, and it is the only Wood Brothers eight-column engine still where it was installed.

name: Tottenham Marshes
text: Your train passes near Tottenham Marshes, on the train's {side}, part of the Lee Valley Park since 1972. Tottenham Hotspur played their first matches there, in 1882, before moving to an enclosed ground.

name: Glover and Main
text: Your train passes near the site of Glover and Main's Gothic Works, on the train's {side}, where gas meters were made from 1897. Thomas Glover had invented the diaphragm gas meter in 1843, and the firm became one of Britain's biggest makers of gas cookers.

name: Wright's Flour Mill
text: Your train passes near Wright's Flour Mill, on the train's {side}, Enfield's oldest working industrial building, with parts dating from 1789. There has been a mill there since at least the late 16th century; the Wright family still own it.

name: Beavertown Brewery
text: Your train passes near Beavertown Brewery, on the train's {side}, founded in 2011 by Logan Plant, son of Led Zeppelin's Robert Plant. Its name comes from De Beauvoir Town, where its first beer was brewed; its Enfield brewery opened in 2020.

name: Enfield Power Station
text: Your train passes near Enfield Power Station, on the train's {side}, a 442-megawatt gas-fired station on part of the site of the old Brimsdown Power Station. Building started in September 1997, and it was running by December 1999.

name: The Eleanor Cross, Waltham Cross
text: Your train passes near the Eleanor Cross at Waltham Cross, on the train's {side}, one of only three of Edward I's crosses for his queen, Eleanor of Castile, still standing. They marked where her coffin rested on its way from Lincoln to Westminster Abbey in 1290; the town is named after it.

name: Lee Valley VeloPark
text: Your train passes near the Lee Valley VeloPark, on the train's {side}, with its velodrome built for the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games. It also has a BMX track, a one-mile road course and five miles of mountain bike trails, and opened to the public in March 2014.

name: St Dunstan's, Stepney
text: Your train passes near St Dunstan's, Stepney, on the train's {side}, believed to have been founded or refounded by St Dunstan in about 952. It is known as the Mother Church of the East End, and as the Church of the High Seas.

name: Trinity Green Almshouses
text: Your train passes near Trinity Green Almshouses, on the train's {side}, built by Trinity House in 1695 for retired sailors and their widows. Saved from demolition in the 1890s by a public campaign, they were the first buildings on the register that grew into today's listed buildings.

name: St Anne's Limehouse
text: Your train passes near St Anne's Limehouse, on the train's {side}, designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor and consecrated in 1730. Being so close to the river, it was given the right to fly the White Ensign of the Royal Navy.

name: Billingsgate Fish Market
text: Your train passes near Billingsgate Fish Market, on the train's {side}, the largest inland fish market in the United Kingdom. It moved here, by the West India Docks, from the City of London in 1982; in the 19th century, Billingsgate was the largest fish market in the world.

name: Woolwich Ferry
text: Your train passes near the Woolwich Ferry, on the train's {side}, a free vehicle and foot ferry across the Thames. A ferry has run at Woolwich since the 14th century; the free service began in 1889, and about two million passengers use it each year.

name: The Royal Arsenal's Grand Store
text: Your train passes near the Royal Arsenal's Grand Store, on the train's {side}, a great three-sided range of riverside warehouses built in 1805 to 1813 to James Wyatt's design. Wooden piles were used instead of the stone foundations he specified, and the buildings suffered from subsidence for many years.

name: St Nicholas Church, Plumstead
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church, Plumstead, on the train's {side}, on a site with a church since about the 10th century. Its oldest part, now the south aisle, is 12th and 13th century, and its tower dates from 1664; it was badly damaged by flying bombs in 1944 and 1945.

name: The site of the Manor Ground
text: Your train passes near the site of the Manor Ground, on the train's {side}, home from 1888 of Royal Arsenal, the club that became Arsenal. The pitch was famously muddy, and with no stands, wagons borrowed from army bases nearby held the crowds.

name: The Royal Brass Foundry
text: Your train passes near the Royal Brass Foundry, on the train's {side}, built for the Board of Ordnance's own gun foundry, set up in 1717. It is tall inside, for a machine that bored cannon upright, and has tall doors to get the new guns out; the foundry was renamed the Royal Gun Factory in 1855.

name: The Valley
text: Your train passes near The Valley, on the train's {side}, home of Charlton Athletic since 1919. Supporters dug out the pitch themselves in an old sand and chalk pit; it now holds 27,111.

name: Morden College
text: Your train passes near Morden College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1695 by Sir John Morden as a home for merchants who had fallen on hard times. Its design is sometimes said to be by Sir Christopher Wren; it is still a retirement home, and its day centre won the Stirling Prize in 2023.

name: Blackheath Quaker Meeting House
text: Your train passes near Blackheath Quaker Meeting House, on the train's {side}, designed by Trevor Dannatt and used by Quakers since 1972. It is thought to be the only Quaker meeting house in Britain built in the Brutalist style, and has been called a “Brutalist jewel”.

name: Telegraph Hill
text: Your train passes near Telegraph Hill, on the train's {side}, once called Plowed Garlic Hill. It takes its name from a semaphore telegraph station built on top in about 1795, one of the points from which news of Wellington's victory at Waterloo was passed to London.

name: Nunhead Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Nunhead Cemetery, on the train's {side}, consecrated in 1840 as All Saints' Cemetery. One of two of London's “Magnificent Seven” Victorian cemeteries south of the Thames, it is now a local nature reserve.

name: Maudsley Hospital
text: Your train passes near the Maudsley Hospital, on the train's {side}, the largest mental health training institution in the UK. The psychiatrist Henry Maudsley offered £30,000 in 1907 towards a hospital for early and acute cases, with teaching and research.

name: House of Dreams
text: Your train passes near the House of Dreams, on the train's {side}, an ordinary terraced house that the designer Stephen Wright has turned into his own art museum since 1998. It is a memorial to his late partner and his parents, and opens to visitors about ten times a year.

name: James Allen's Girls' School
text: Your train passes near James Allen's Girls' School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1741 and the second-oldest independent girls' school in Great Britain. It began as part of Edward Alleyn's charity, with Dulwich College and Alleyn's School.

name: Herne Hill Velodrome
text: Your train passes near Herne Hill Velodrome, on the train's {side}, built in 1891 and one of the oldest cycle tracks in the world. It hosted the track cycling at the 1948 Olympics, and Crystal Palace football club played there during the First World War.

name: Streatham Ice and Leisure Centre
text: Your train passes near Streatham Ice and Leisure Centre, on the train's {side}, London's only Olympic-sized ice rink and home of the Streatham ice hockey teams. It replaced Streatham Ice Arena, opened on the site on February 26th 1931.

name: St Barnabas' Church, Mitcham
text: Your train passes near St Barnabas' Church, Mitcham, on the train's {side}, designed by H. P. Burke Downing and finished on November 14th 1914. It replaced a simple one-room “tin church” used by the mission set up there in 1906.

name: Wandle Meadow Nature Park
text: Your train passes near Wandle Meadow Nature Park, on the train's {side}, beside the River Wandle. Part of a sewage works from 1877 to 1970, it was proposed as a site for a Wimbledon football stadium, but local people opposed it and it became a nature reserve in 1989.

name: The site of Plough Lane
text: Your train passes near the site of Plough Lane, on the train's {side}, Wimbledon Football Club's ground from September 1912 until 1991. It was demolished in 2002, and the houses built there are named Reynolds Gate after the Wimbledon striker Eddie Reynolds.

name: The Bedford, Balham
text: Your train passes near The Bedford in Balham, on the train's {side}, a listed pub rebuilt in about 1931 and known for comedy and music. The Clash, U2 and Ed Sheeran have all played early gigs there.
